speechtext: I thought I had explained that point clearly. There are 31 officers in a battalion. There has been an accumulation of officers in England, ap-* parently because of the fact the casualties have been proportionately heavier amongst the rank and file than amongst the officers. Otherwise, that accumulation of officers would not have occurred. There ie, I suppose, another reason: the policy adopted in the British and Canadian armies is to grant commissions on the field to competent men, Many a splendid fellow goes out from Canada who has not seen service in the trenches. It is a question whether it is advisable to put such a man over the head of a sergeant, for instance, or other non-commissioned officer, who has been in France for a year or two and has done splendid service.

maintopic: CLASSIFIED TABLE OF DISCHARGES IN THE C.E.F. FROM THE COMMENCEMENT
speechtext: The non-commissioned officers are brought back for training.

maintopic: CLASSIFIED TABLE OF DISCHARGES IN THE C.E.F. FROM THE COMMENCEMENT
speechtext:
Certainly. To some extent-not altogether-that may account for the condition referred to.
The member for West Middlesex (Mr. Ross) refers to the large number of persons who are employed in the pay and records office in England and in the assigned pay and separation allowance branch here. But the hon. gentleman must remember that it is not fair to compare the number of employees in the pay and records office in England with the number of employees in the assigned pay and separation allowance branch here. We have
,TULY 6, 1917
the records branch in Ottawa, which is separate from the assigned pay and separation allowance branch. We have about 600 clerks in the records office-many of them work nights as well as during the day-and 600 or 700 in the other offices.

maintopic: CLASSIFIED TABLE OF DISCHARGES IN THE C.E.F. FROM THE COMMENCEMENT
speechtext: Twice too many in both.

maintopic: CLASSIFIED TABLE OF DISCHARGES IN THE C.E.F. FROM THE COMMENCEMENT
speechtext:
I often hear assertions of that kind from my hon. friends opposite. I wish that these hon. gentlemen would take time to inform themselves by going round and seeing what is being done in these offices. If they did they would not come to iany such conclusions as that which my hon. friend has apparently reached. There is a staff of faithful, honest workers in the department at Ottawa. At the heads of these staffs are competent, conscientious men. When I discuss with them matters connected with their different branches, I find that they are anxious to serve the public to the best of their ability. Many of these men were in the department before the war broke out and had to take charge of much wider work in the different branches. They have performed land are performing a splendid service. I do not believe that there is a surplus of employees; I do not think the member for West Middlesex is justified in saying that there is, nor do I think that he can produce evidence to prove his assertion. I should be glad to produce evidence that he is mistaken in that regard. There is a tremendous amount of work in looking after the details connected with the 400,000 men, sending out thousands of cheques every month, adjusting the accounts, and so on. Our men are scattered all over this continent; they are in England and in France. They move around from place to place, their addresses change. Unfortunately, some of them are killed; others are wounded. When the men are wounded they are transferred to a hospital in France. From there they may he transferred to a hospital in Ehgland, and they may be further transferred to Canada. All these movements involve a certain amount of w(ork in the records office. Then, the families of some of these men have gone to England, and have forgotten to give their addresses. This sort of thing involves attention to a tremendous amount of detail. I am informed that the employees in the offices in England are mostly female employees; any men who are employed are unfit for other kinds of military service. According to this sheet to which reference has been made, there are 42 male employees in the Canadian Records
Office. It is probable that more males are employed in the records office than that, but they are attached to other units in the service. I assure my hon. friend that no able-bodied men would be employed to do clerical work-unless his services were indispensable-if he was fit for more important military duties.

maintopic: CLASSIFIED TABLE OF DISCHARGES IN THE C.E.F. FROM THE COMMENCEMENT
speechtext: I do not want to criticise the minister unduly; I know that his duties are very onerous and that the times are trying. But I am informed by officers returned from England that the condition of the Pay and Records Office there is an open scandal; that the employees are so numerous that they are simply falling over each other. I would be much obliged if the minister would furnish me with information as to the number of persons employed in the Pay and Records Office, their sex, and how many officers of the militia are employed, if any, who have seen active service. I should be glad if he would give me the general details in regard to the matter. If my criticism is unjust, I shall be only too glad to retract it.

speakerposition: Prime Minister; Secretary of State for External Affairs; President of the Privy Council
maintopic: CLASSIFIED TABLE OF DISCHARGES IN THE C.E.F. FROM THE COMMENCEMENT
speechtext:
We will endeavour to get the information for my hon. friend. But I really think that hon. gentlemen should take care to be well informed before they cast aspersions upon men who are just as upright and have just as good a status in the community in which they have hitherto lived as any hon. gentleman in this committee. I did not see the Pay and Record Office this year. I know that the Minister of Marine and Fisheries visited the office and he told me that his visit indicated to him that the work was being carried on in a most satisfactory and systematic manner, and he was very much impressed with it. That was the impression I derived when I visited the Pay and Records Office in 1915. I do not think any hon. gentleman in this House has much conception of the quantity of work that is done there. How many thousand inquiries does my hon. friend imagine are made in that office every day in the year about the men, 300,000 or thereabouts, who are in the United Kingdom or in France? The complications which call for these inquiries are very considerable. Reference has been made to the hospitals. Wounded men are very often moved horn one hospital to another, and the clerks in the Pay and Records office have to keep an exact account of when a man leaves a hospital and where he goes to, They have to keep an account of transfers from one battalion to another, from

one service to another. There are thousands of details.

speechtext: The estates of the dead.

speechtext: That ie a separate department.

speechtext: The next of kin of some pooir man who has been killed may live in Switzerland, or Norway, or Russia, oir Italy, or somewhere else. The officer has to make arrangements with the Governments "of those countries for all the formalities in connection with the administration, so that the Government of Canada can get a good discharge. In just that one respect alone that has been brought to. my attention by the hon. member of Victoria (Sir Sam Hughes), the work is enormous, and the legal complexities that this officer has to deal with are by no means inconsiderable. This gentleman was a lawyer who. had gone overseas in the Expeditionary Force, and he had eventually been transferred to these duties, because they were important, and he was very well qualified to fulfil them. I must confess I should gravely doubt whether there is any room for the criticism which my hon. friend has put forward, but we will make some inquiries. It is most undesirable, I am sure my hon. friend will agree, that men who have been taken from the best communities in this .country, men having as good a status and as good .a reputation as any man in this House, should be subjected to undeserved aspersions, and I am not disposed to accept them unless some better evidence is brought to my attention. Colonel Ross is a man at the head of his profession.

maintopic: CLASSIFIED TABLE OF DISCHARGES IN THE C.E.F. FROM THE COMMENCEMENT
speechtext: That is a good name.

speakerposition: Prime Minister; Secretary of State for External Affairs; President of the Privy Council
maintopic: CLASSIFIED TABLE OF DISCHARGES IN THE C.E.F. FROM THE COMMENCEMENT
speechtext:
It is a good
name, and it deserves better treatment from my hon. friend from West Middlesex than to have aspersions cast upon it witih-

out sufficient evidence. Colonel Ross, so far as my information goes, is a man of the highest character. He is the best man that the then Minister of Militia (Sir Sam Hughes) could find for the very important duties which are entrusted to him. He has gone over to England, and so far as I could observe, he has discharged those duties with the utmost fidelity, ability and energy. I hope my hon. friend will not take for granted all those rumours, some of which have come to my attention through the press. It is the easiest thing in the world to exaggerate rumours, and, of course, they acquire a considerable importance when they are quoted by a member of the House. I have no information that would lead me to suppose that they are correct.

maintopic: CLASSIFIED TABLE OF DISCHARGES IN THE C.E.F. FROM THE COMMENCEMENT
speechtext: I admit frankly that in 1915 the Pay and Records Office was all upside down. I then appointed a very prominent auditor who put things in proper shape. I later on appointed Colonel Ross to go over and take charge. Later on the Auditor General went over, expecting to find something wrong, but he reported that things were, to his surprise, in ship-shape order. The reason for the trouble to which my hon. friend refers is this. There is more or less truth about the mistakes being made because many of the clerks are soldiers who, after having served at the front and having been wounded, have returned, to England and are employed in the Pay and Record Office to take the place of men who have become convalescent and fit for service again, and have gone to the front. These lads require two or three weeks training in order to learn the business. That is the condition that I found last year was the chief cause of the trouble, namely, these men making mistakes before they understood the routine of the work.

maintopic: CLASSIFIED TABLE OF DISCHARGES IN THE C.E.F. FROM THE COMMENCEMENT
speechtext:
I would not want the Prime Minister to think I was endeavouring to cast any aspersion on any persons, nor that 1 would make the statement that I have made on information I have personally. I must candidly say, however, that I have heard statements to the effect that I have described, made, not once nor twice, but many times, by officers of high standing in the 'Canadian Expeditionary Force of just as good character and just as reliable as even the Minister of Marine and Fisheries. I hope the statements are not true. If the matter is looked into, and if the Prime Minister will kindly furnish me the information for which I have asked with regard to the encumbering of that branch

with an excessive number of employees, I would like to have it.

maintopic: CLASSIFIED TABLE OF DISCHARGES IN THE C.E.F. FROM THE COMMENCEMENT
speechtext: My hon. friend does not impute any dishonesty on the part of the employees?

maintopic: CLASSIFIED TABLE OF DISCHARGES IN THE C.E.F. FROM THE COMMENCEMENT
speechtext: Not at all, but statements have been made to the effect that the department is over-manned.

maintopic: CLASSIFIED TABLE OF DISCHARGES IN THE C.E.F. FROM THE COMMENCEMENT
speechtext:
I would like to bring to the attention of the House the information which I have here bearing on the subject that was under discussion a few minutes ago in regard to the number of unfit men in England and how they got there. Dr. Bruce's report, which has been laid upon the Table and which is a public document, begins with this statement:
Many hundreds of soldiers obviously unfit for service overseas have been sent from Canada to England.
The report of Dr. Jones, who was in charge of the medical service, and on the discharge of whose duties Dr. Bruce reported, says:
There is no question of doubt that a large number of men have been sent over from Canada who must have been medically unfit when they were enlisted. This has resulted in an unnecessary burden being thrown on the medical and other services in England that deal with the weeding out of these men and their disposal.
The report of the BaJbtie Commission which investigated Dr. Bruce's report deals with the same subject also in its first paragraph.
The Board is agreed that large numbers of soldiers have come, and continue to come, from Canada who are unfit for service at the front.
Dr. Bruce's report is dated September 20, 1916; Surgeon-General Jones' report, September 28, 1916, and the Babtie report December 22, 1916. So the different authorities are absolutely agreed upon the existence of the condition, and they all agree that it is very far-reaching. I have ,an opinion here which I shall take the liberty of reading to the House as to how far-reaching this condition is. It alleges that:
The number of soldiers arriving in England from Canada physically unfit for service at the front is steadily growing.

maintopic: CLASSIFIED TABLE OF DISCHARGES IN THE C.E.F. FROM THE COMMENCEMENT
speechtext: What report is that?

maintopic: CLASSIFIED TABLE OF DISCHARGES IN THE C.E.F. FROM THE COMMENCEMENT
speechtext:
This is not a report. It is information that I have at hand and is dated October 27, 1916. It goes on:
In the case of twelve battalions recently arrived the number has reached the serious proportion of over 16 per cent. The medical
examination of these men has shown that the great majority of them have for a long time been suffering from obvious physical disabilities and should never have been enlisted. These unfits by reason of their disabilities form an undue proportion of the patients in hospitals in England, and are thus placing a heavy strain on the medical service. They present a very serious question from the pensions point of view owing to the very great difficulty of establishing the facts as to whether the disabilities were the result of, or aggravated by military service. These men who are not suitable for active military service are nevertheless capable of productive work in Canada, and practically all of them were taken from productive work in Canada and enlisted in military service for which they are useless at enormous expense to the Government, so that not only has the value of their labour been lost to the country, but they have been a heavy charge during their period of service without giving any return.
The Babtie report not only agrees with the Bruce and the Jones reports as to the conditions existing, but gives the reasons why those conditions exist, and this is a mattpr which I think should be placed before the House and the country.
The Board is satisfied that there have been large numbers of men passed who ought not to have been passed by the medical officers, but it was, perhaps inevitable under the circumstances of raising the Canadian Expeditionary Force that examinations could not be conducted with all the care necessary. This it believes to have been due partly to inexperience on the part of examining medical officers, partly to hurry, partly to carelessness, and lastly, in some instances, to -the opinion of the examining medical officer being overridden or ignored by ' commanding officers. These defects in recruiting continue to exist, despite medical examinations by recruiting medical officers, by battalion medical officers on joining units, and before sailing for the United Kingdom.
To show the extent to which this improper passing of the medically unfit has taken place, I will cite an instance or two from the Bruce report, which I think the House will find somewhat startling. Dr. Bruce gives a number of pages of unfits where the cases are described by name, regimental number, and place of enlistment. The first one I will cite is:
No. 602397, Pte. W. J. Clements of the 34th Battalion, age SO years, 79 years when enlisted at Guelph, March 19, 1915. Disability, advanced hardening of the arteries, examined by Major Ratz, Guelph.
The other case is:
Pte. R. Mick No. 297454, enlisted with 224th Battalion March 17, 1916, at Pembroke, Ont. He is 16 years of age, weighs 80 pounds only, undeveloped and weak muscles in the right hip and thigh. He was passed by a doctor at Pembroke and was again examined and passed by a military medical officer at Quebec. On both occasions he says he was stripped and passed as medically fit. He left Canada three

weeks after enlistment and has been in a hospital in England most of the time since arriving, suffering from his legs.
I again draw attention to the Babtie report, which says:
The ineffiicent character of the medical examination in some instances is clue to the opinion of the examining medical officer being overridden or ignored by commanding officers.
I think the evidence there is absolute that the commanding officer was exercising his authority not as a military man but as a man having political pull. We have in that fact a very great part of the reason why recruiting conditions in Canada are as they are. Certainly we have the evidence of the Babtie Commission that that is one large part of the reason why we are carrying on the military strength in England to-day thousands, if not tens of thousands, of men who are absolutely unfit for military service.

maintopic: CLASSIFIED TABLE OF DISCHARGES IN THE C.E.F. FROM THE COMMENCEMENT
speechtext: The 224th Battalion which my hon. friend mentioned is commanded, I believe, by one of the best Grits in the Dominion.

maintopic: CLASSIFIED TABLE OF DISCHARGES IN THE C.E.F. FROM THE COMMENCEMENT
speechtext: It makes no difference who commands it. The point is what he did.

maintopic: CLASSIFIED TABLE OF DISCHARGES IN THE C.E.F. FROM THE COMMENCEMENT
speechtext: How would he get his political pull if he was a Grit?

maintopic: CLASSIFIED TABLE OF DISCHARGES IN THE C.E.F. FROM THE COMMENCEMENT
speechtext: I cannot answer that.

maintopic: CLASSIFIED TABLE OF DISCHARGES IN THE C.E.F. FROM THE COMMENCEMENT
speechtext: I think his name is Alec McDougall.

maintopic: CLASSIFIED TABLE OF DISCHARGES IN THE C.E.F. FROM THE COMMENCEMENT
speechtext: It makes no difference what his name is. In that particular case it might have been because the medical officer got his appointment by political pull, and was incompetent, pr as the Babtie report says, "in a hurry or careless."

maintopic: CLASSIFIED TABLE OF DISCHARGES IN THE C.E.F. FROM THE COMMENCEMENT
speechtext: It might also be that he was one of the 80 per cent of Grit doctors appointed.

maintopic: CLASSIFIED TABLE OF DISCHARGES IN THE C.E.F. FROM THE COMMENCEMENT
speechtext:
It makes no; difference
whether they were Grit doctors or Grit colonels. This Government is responsible, and the Minister of Militia is directly responsible, for the conduct of our military forces. That is the condition that exists and that has existed, and the Government and the Minister of Militia are responsible for it. And out of that condition grows- as it of necessity must grow-the dissatisfaction with the management of our military affairs, which, again, results in the depression of military enthusiasm that we find throughout the country at the present time.

maintopic: CLASSIFIED TABLE OF DISCHARGES IN THE C.E.F. FROM THE COMMENCEMENT
speechtext: That was my work last year in England-to get this medical business on as satisfactory a basis as I could.

maintopic: CLASSIFIED TABLE OF DISCHARGES IN THE C.E.F. FROM THE COMMENCEMENT
speechtext: I am not finding fault with the former minister's efforts to make things right. I say that study of the Bruce report shows that Dr. Bruce was most energetic, and, so far as a dayman can judge from reading it, most efficient. What may have been the family troubles in the Government I am hot prepared to say, but, apparently. Dr. Bruce's report was not allowed to come into effect. He was investigated, and the result of that investigation was the Babtie report, and Dr. Bruce is not in the service of the Dominion of Canada to-day.

maintopic: CLASSIFIED TABLE OF DISCHARGES IN THE C.E.F. FROM THE COMMENCEMENT
speechtext: The hon. gentleman (Mr. Oliver) is well acquainted with conditions in the Edmonton district. Does he know of cases of this political influence of which he speaks in that district?

maintopic: CLASSIFIED TABLE OF DISCHARGES IN THE C.E.F. FROM THE COMMENCEMENT
speechtext: I am not here to answer questions about the conditions in Edmonton.

maintopic: CLASSIFIED TABLE OF DISCHARGES IN THE C.E.F. FROM THE COMMENCEMENT
speechtext:
But the hon. gentleman is making a charge that it was because of political influence that a large number of men got past the local medical officers. So,
I ask if he knows anything about political pull having been used in his own district concerning which he is well informed. My information is that the' medical officers generally did not belong to the political party of the Government, but rather to the other party.

maintopic: CLASSIFIED TABLE OF DISCHARGES IN THE C.E.F. FROM THE COMMENCEMENT
speechtext:
I am not discussing matters in Edmonton. I brought up two instances, one in Guelph and the other in Pembroke. It was not necessary to refer to Edmonton;
I think that perhaps the same conditions did not exist there. But, looking over the Bruce report I found such scandalous cases as those to which I have referred. I am not discussing the locality, but the fact as reported. I am not giving my opinion to the House, I am giving the statements made in the report ,of the Babtie Commission, which shows that certain conditions existed partly because of the inefficiency of the medical men, or, possibly, because of the decisions ,of the medical	men,	being .overridden by the
commanding officers. I say this is a condition for which the military administration of the Dominion must accept full responsibility. I bring it to the attention of the Minister of Militia on this occasion, and

I hope we shall hear further from him with regard to it.

maintopic: CLASSIFIED TABLE OF DISCHARGES IN THE C.E.F. FROM THE COMMENCEMENT
speechtext:
Before the committee rises, I have a suggestion to make. This Bill has been under discussion for two weeks. To-day's sitting has been quite argumentative, and yesterday's was exhausting.
I understand that a great number of members are out of town. It seems to me therefore ,that we might well postpone further consideration of this Bill until Monday morning and, for the balance of the week, take up other business. I think that, on the whole, our progress will :be just as great. And possibly the Prime Minister might consider the suggestion pf an adjournment now.

maintopic: CLASSIFIED TABLE OF DISCHARGES IN THE C.E.F. FROM THE COMMENCEMENT
speechtext:
Along similar lines,
I was going to take the liberty of suggesting that members who have suggestions to make for changes in the Bill might make them in writing to the Minister pf Militia, or to the Minister of Justice for their consideration, and so avoid taking up more time than is necessary with discussion in this committee. My object is to get on with the Bill with the least possible delay. Let us get through the Bill as soon as we can. If my suggestion were adopted, progress would be made with the Bill even though the consideration pf it in this committee were not proceeded with until Monday.

speechtext:
Has my right
hon. friend (Sir Wilfrid Laurier) opposite anything to suggest?

maintopic: CLASSIFIED TABLE OF DISCHARGES IN THE C.E.F. FROM THE COMMENCEMENT
speechtext:
I hope that
the Prime Minister will be content tp have the House adjourn now.

speakerposition: Prime Minister; Secretary of State for External Affairs; President of the Privy Council
maintopic: CLASSIFIED TABLE OF DISCHARGES IN THE C.E.F. FROM THE COMMENCEMENT
speechtext: I am quite prepared to go on this evening, and so far as I am concerned. I should be glad to do so. At the same time, I do not wish to insist upon my own view. To-day we have not touched any of the clauses of the Bill, the time having been occupied with general discussion-and I suppose that general discussion is necessary, though much of what has gone on this afternoon has not been relevant to the Bill. I am prepared to adjourn now. I should like to go on tomorrow, and especially to get through with clauses of the Bill that are not controversial. There must be some of a formal character which might be passed, and thus some progress would made. If we come to clauses which are controversial or as to which information is desired, they can be allowed to stand for the time being.

maintopic: CLASSIFIED TABLE OF DISCHARGES IN THE C.E.F. FROM THE COMMENCEMENT
speechtext: There will be just a general consideration of the Bill to-morrow, I suppose?

speakerposition: Prime Minister; Secretary of State for External Affairs; President of the Privy Council
maintopic: CLASSIFIED TABLE OF DISCHARGES IN THE C.E.F. FROM THE COMMENCEMENT
speechtext:
I should prefer that those clauses that are not controversial should be passed, I should like to make some progress with the Bill which has been before the House every day for two weeks. With that understanding, I am willing that the House should adjourn.
Progress reported.

Saturday, July 7, 1917.
